name: Face taping (Frownies / sleep patches)

lead: Face taping means sticking paper or tape patches over expression lines on the forehead, between the brows and around the eyes and mouth, usually overnight, to soften those lines.

The patch acts as a stiff splint that holds skin flat and limits muscle creasing while it is worn, and proponents say consistent use softens lines over weeks or months. Frownies, a brand dating to 1889 by its own account, is the best-known version; it describes the effect as temporary and dependent on ongoing use. No published trials of face-taping patches were found.

paras: People apply the patches to clean skin before bed, over the lines they want to soften, and remove them in the morning. Frownies use a water-activated adhesive. Users wear them regularly over weeks.
As with any adhesive on skin, irritation is possible, especially on sensitive skin. Patches are sold as cosmetics rather than medical devices, and no safety studies were found.

web.title: Does face taping for wrinkles work? (NBC News Select)

angle.text: Users wear paper or tape patches overnight on the forehead, between the brows and around the eyes and mouth to soften expression lines. The patch holds skin flat so muscles crease it less during sleep. Frownies has sold them for over a century.

lead: Face taping is the practice of applying adhesive patches or tape to the face to hold skin flat, either overnight to limit creasing from expression and sleep, or in a pull-up style for an instant lift at the temples, cheeks or jawline.[1][2] The best-known product is Frownies, an American brand of paper patches with a water-activated adhesive.[3] People use it to soften forehead lines, the vertical "11" lines between the brows, crow's feet and lines around the mouth, and to look smoother for photos and events.[3][1]

Proponents say holding the skin still and limiting muscle movement while the patch is worn can soften expression lines over weeks of regular use. The manufacturer describes the effect as temporary and dependent on ongoing use.[3] Dermatologist Anetta Reszko told NBC News it is "a temporary solution" that gives immediate smoothing, and that overnight use may reduce sleep creases.[1]

The practice went viral on social media, and brands such as Frownies report renewed interest through TikTok.[3] No clinical trial of face-taping patches has been published; commentary comes from dermatologists and plastic surgeons, who describe it as affecting dynamic wrinkles (from repeated movement) temporarily while static wrinkles, visible at rest, are not addressed.[1][2]
infobox: Unbleached Kraft paper with starch-based (dextrin) adhesive [3]
Forehead, between the brows, eye and mouth corners [3]

paras: Frownies patches are made of weighted, unbleached Kraft paper coated with a hypoallergenic, vegetable-derived adhesive that activates when wetted and hardens, giving the patch a stiff, cast-like quality [3]. The manufacturer sells triangular patches for the forehead and between the eyes, and diamond and butterfly shapes for the corners of the eyes and mouth. A separate line, Gentle Lifts, uses smaller self-adhesive cotton-lined patches for fine areas such as lip lines [3].

The company describes the mechanism as mechanical rather than chemical: the patch acts as a splint that keeps the skin and muscle in a relaxed, flat position, with no active ingredient involved [3]. Some other products marketed as sleep patches or wrinkle tapes use silicone or medical-style tape to the same end.

According to the company's account, the product was invented in 1889 by Margaret Kroesen for her daughter Alice, a concert pianist and model who developed frown lines from furrowing her brow. It was originally sold as 'Wrinkle Eradicators' [3]. The business describes itself as family-owned and led by women across five generations, with fifth-generation leadership taking over in 2025 [3]. The brand reports renewed popularity through social media, including TikTok [3]. These historical details come from an AI-generated summary of company material and have not been independently verified.

The brand positions the patches as a non-invasive, drug-free alternative to injections such as botulinum toxin.[3] Medical references describe botulinum toxin as working by immobilising the muscles that produce wrinkles, which is the same stated principle behind taping, though the two act through different means.[4]

Reszko says taping may help retrain muscles to move less forcefully and so reduce dynamic wrinkles, but not static ones, and that it does not rebuild collagen.[1] An Ochsner Health clinician article says taping can smooth fine lines right after removal but that lines often return within hours and deep wrinkles generally are not helped, and names injectables from a certified professional and daily sunscreen as longer-term approaches.[2]
Wrinkles are attributed in medical sources to many factors, including sun damage, smoking, glycation, sleep position and repeated facial expression.[4]

Reszko says tape that is not skin-friendly can damage the skin barrier and cause irritation or contact dermatitis, especially around the eyes and mouth, and recommends medical-grade silicone tape; plastic surgeon Kristy Hamilton warns repeated pulling may make the face look saggier once the tape is off.[1] Ochsner Health says taping is not considered harmful for most people but that repeated application and removal can irritate the outer skin layer, and that experts advise against using it daily.[2]

A looksmax.org thread titled "Face-taping, the next potential looksmax?" proposes that facial sagging and under-eye circles after short sleep reflect skin stretching under gravity, and argues that taping could counter this by applying mechanical tension in a chosen direction.[5] The poster also suggests mouth taping might reduce lower-face bloat and add fullness to the upper face; another reply questions the thread's quality, and no published study tests these ideas.[5]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org face taping is discussed as a possible cheap, non-invasive way to alter facial fullness and sagging, alongside mouth taping and other mechanical-pressure ideas.[5]

claims.claim: Taping holds skin in a better position and reverses sagging, bloat and under-eye circles.
Overnight patches soften expression lines over time.
Taping is a gentle substitute for botulinum toxin.

timeline.event: Margaret Kroesen creates adhesive patches later sold as 'Wrinkle Eradicators' / Frownies, per the company [3]
